blocks.en: A first concern is that the prompt text alone might predict failure. Failure is frequent on every model (rates of .365 to .688 per failure type) and varies widely: of the 72 type-category-model cells, five are at or below .10 and four at or above .90 (Appendix F ). To test this, we tried to predict which prompts fail using only quantities that can be computed from the prompt text, without running the video model. We used three kinds of quantity: five measures of how complex the prompt is (its length, the numbers of words and of entities, the number of modifiers, and the depth of its sentence structure); a rating r r , given by a language model, of how rare the described scene is in the real world; and the distance u u between p p and p ∘ p^{\circ} in the text encoder that the video model uses (definitions in Appendix C ). We score each predictor by its AUROC, which answers the following question: if we pick one failing prompt and one succeeding prompt at random, how often does the predictor give the failing one the higher score? A value of .500 means the predictor is no better than guessing. With all text-only predictors combined, AUROC is 0.607/0.635/0.694 on the three models when the three failure types are pooled. These pooled values overstate what the predictors can do, because the pooled model also knows which failure type each prompt belongs to, and the failure types differ in how often they fail. Within a single failure type the predictors do much worse: for rare composition they are at the level of guessing on two of three models (.520, .523), and among temporal prompts they stay below .65 throughout. The rarity rating fails because the suite holds real-world rarity nearly constant (63% of rare-composition prompts are rated 6 or 7 of 7) while failure varies from prompt to prompt. The encoder distance u u is the closest text-only counterpart of demand: it compares the same two prompts, p p and p ∘ p^{\circ} , in the same text encoder, and differs from demand only in never running the video denoiser. Within rare composition and within temporal prompts its AUROC is .44 to .55, no better than guessing. What demand captures is therefore not present in the text encoder’s representation of the prompt; it arises only when the denoiser processes the prompt. In negation the text-only predictors appear to work well (.771 to .824). The reason is that the negation suite has eight categories with very different failure rates, and the wording of a prompt reveals its category, so the predictors are recognizing the category and not separating failing from succeeding prompts within one. In short, the text of a prompt does not tell us whether it will fail; that has to be read from the model.

blocks.en: Demand adds predictive power beyond these baselines, though modestly (Table 2 b). Added to all text-only predictors with a single slope, demand gains + 0.025 +0.025 , + 0.056 +0.056 , + 0.001 +0.001 AUROC on the three models. A single slope averages a positive correlation (negation) with negative ones (the other two), so it understates the signal, and on CogVideoX the two cancel. With one slope per failure type the gain is + 0.050 +0.050 , + 0.104 +0.104 , + 0.011 +0.011 . The cleanest test is inside rare composition with category fixed effects, where text alone reaches .588/.748/.689 and adding demand gives .628/.782/.739, a gain on all three models. Excluding clips the judge found ambiguous reproduces the pattern ( + .026 / + .056 / + .002 +.026/+.056/+.002 pooled). We do not propose demand as a standalone classifier: whether a given prompt fails also depends on the random seed, which caps what any prompt-level score can reach. Demand thus carries information that no text-only predictor has. It is best used, together with the failure type, to decide what to try after a failure, and not as a detector that says in advance whether a single prompt will fail.

blocks.en: Demand measured on one model predicts untreated failure on another, even though which prompts fail is partly model-specific: the correlation ϕ \phi of per-prompt failure between two models is .48 for negation and only .16 to .26 for rare composition, so whether a snowy beach fails depends on which model is asked. In the pooled transfer matrix (Table 15 ), every off-diagonal AUROC lies within 0.03 of the same-model value in its column (0.577/0.617/0.631). Demand therefore measures something that the models share, whereas the conditions under which raising the scale helps differ from model to model (Appendix J ). For this reason both should be measured on the model that is actually in use.

One could worry that the link between demand and recovery is circular for TPD, whose correction direction coincides with ϵ text − ϵ ∘ \epsilon_{\text{text}}-\epsilon^{\circ} for temporal prompts. Three facts rule it out: demand is measured on untreated runs and recovery on treated outputs; the same relation holds for corrections whose direction differs from that difference and for scale-up, which adds no direction at all; and demand predicts untreated failure on models where no correction ever runs (Appendix O ). The relation is an empirical result and not a by-product of how one correction is built.

blocks.en: A last concern is that the three suites use three judges. To check that they measure one thing, a single judge asked one question of every clip: does it show p ∘ p^{\circ} rather than p p ? We compared the two sets of labels on 201 clips, chosen so that every model, failure type, category, and label is represented (a stratified sample). Agreement is measured with Cohen’s κ \kappa , which is 0 when two judges agree no more often than they would by chance and 1 when they always agree. We obtain κ = 0.49 \kappa=0.49 overall (0.41 to 0.59 per failure type), a moderate level of agreement. To understand the disagreements, we use the fact that the original judges also give each clip a graded score before deciding between failure and success. Clips on which the two judgments disagree have a middle score far more often than clips on which they agree (49% of disagreeing clips against 23% of agreeing ones; Mann-Whitney test, which compares two groups of scores without assuming how they are distributed, p = 1.1 × 10 − 4 p=1.1\times 10^{-4} ). In other words, the judgments disagree mainly on borderline clips, in which the video partly follows the prompt and a yes-or-no label is hard to assign. The two judgments thus measure the same thing and differ only in where they draw the line on such clips, so all analyses above use each suite’s original judgment (Appendix E ). The three suites’ labels therefore answer the same question and failure rates can be compared across failure types, although borderline clips remain a source of noise.
blocks.zh: 最后一项关切是,三个套房使用三名法官。 为了检查他们是否测量了一件事,一个法官问了每个片段的一个问题:它显示的是p Q 而不是p ? 我们比较了201片段上的两套标签,选择了这些标签,以便每个模型、故障类型、类别和标签都得到体现(一个分级样本)。 当两位法官同意的频率不比偶然的多时, 我们总共获得0.49\kappa=0.49(每一次故障为0.41到0.59)这一中等水平的协议。 为了理解分歧,我们利用这样一个事实,即最初的法官在决定失败和成功之间之前也给每个片段一个分级的分数. 两个判决有分歧的剪辑比他们同意的剪辑多得多(49%的剪辑有分歧,23%同意的剪辑有分歧;Mann-Whitney测试,它比较了两组分数,而没有假设分数如何分配,p=1.1×10−4 p=1.1\times 10^{-4}). 换句话说,判决主要在边线剪辑上有分歧,其中视频部分跟随提示,而"是"或"否"标签很难指定. 因此,两项判决在衡量相同情况时不同,只在这些短片上划线时不同,因此上述所有分析都采用每个套件的原始判断(附录E)。 因此,三个套件的标签可以回答同样的问题,故障率可以跨故障类型进行比较,尽管边框夹片仍然是噪音的来源.
